title: The Hungry House
premise: Elodie Lockridge has spent her adult life mapping the unmappable, a habit born from a childhood spent at her grandmother's house in Hollow Creek, where an imaginary friend named Wren taught her that the house eats what it loves. When her grandmother dies and Elodie returns for the funeral, Wren is waiting on the porch — unchanged after thirty years — and the tunnels Elodie once explored beneath the property are revealed to be the house's digestive tract, fed by a bargain struck in 1974 when her grandmother traded her husband's life for her daughter's. To break the cycle, Elodie must return what was taken: not the bones the house hoards, but the original promise itself, spoken aloud at the hearth where the bargain was made. She succeeds only by offering the house her documentation — every map, every recording, the proof the house ever existed — starving it of witness until it forgets itself, though the price is that no one, including Elodie, will remember Hollow Creek or the people it consumed.
about_author: Ivo Delacroix is the pen name of a former land surveyor who spent a decade mapping decommissioned infrastructure across the American Rust Belt before turning to fiction. Their work draws on abandoned-place archives and family oral histories, and they claim to have never entered a basement they didn't immediately regret.

chapters.title: The Cartographer's Prayer
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In present-day Detroit, Elodie documents a forgotten storm tunnel, narrating her belief that documentation is a form of prayer. She receives word of her grandmother's death and an unexpected inheritance notice for the house in Hollow Creek. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness cracked open by grief.

chapters.title: What the Survey Missed
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Packing her archival kit, Elodie rereads her childhood field notebooks and finds pages she doesn't remember writing — maps of tunnels beneath the Hollow Creek house, dated 1994. Emotional beat: unease dressed as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: The Porch Light Was Always On
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. She arrives at the house at dusk. On the porch sits Wren, her childhood imaginary friend, unchanged — same yellow raincoat, same too-wide smile. Wren says, 'You came back to finish it.' Emotional beat: terror and homesickness fused into one.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Haunted Estate
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie catalogues the house's contents, finding her grandmother's locked study, a wall of photographs with faces scratched out, and a 1974 newspaper clipping about a man who vanished. Wren watches from every window. Emotional beat: the house as a museum of erasures.

chapters.title: Wren Remembers Everything
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, the first of several. Wren explains it has waited because the house cannot digest a promise, only people. It warns Elodie not to open the study until she's 'hungry enough to understand.' Emotional beat: affection that curdles into menace.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Won't Look at the House
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elderly neighbor Ruth Pell warns Elodie to sell and leave, revealing that in 1974 Elodie's grandfather, Thomas, disappeared and the family never spoke of it again. Ruth's dog refuses to cross the property line. Emotional beat: the town's complicit silence.

chapters.title: Tunnel One: Where the Floors Go
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Following her childhood maps, Elodie finds a hatch behind the pantry and descends into tunnels that match her 1994 drawings exactly — including a chamber wallpapered with family portraits. Emotional beat: vindication turning to dread as the map proves itself.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie forces the study and finds her grandmother's ledger: decades of entries recording 'feedings' — dates, names, and small offerings that kept the house satisfied. The last entry is Elodie's own childhood name. Emotional beat: betrayal by the person she loved most.

chapters.title: The Bargain of 1974
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth recounts what she witnessed: young Marion Lockridge, desperate to save her sick daughter, made a bargain at the hearth with something under the floor. The house took Thomas instead and demanded a debt renewed each generation. Emotional beat: horror as inheritance.

chapters.title: Wren's First Hunger
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reveals its origin: it was a real child, the Lockridges' neighbor's son, taken in 1974 and remade as the house's mouth and messenger. It has been Wren ever since, and it is tired. Emotional beat: pity entangled with fear.

chapters.title: The House Feeds on Witness
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie tests a theory: when she stops documenting, the house shifts — rooms migrate, tunnels reroute. When she photographs and records, the house holds still. The house needs to be seen to keep what it takes. Emotional beat: the hunter realizing the prey's weakness.

chapters.title: Phone Call from a Dead Line
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At 3 a.m., the disconnected landline rings. Her grandmother's voice recites the ledger entry for Elodie's name and says, 'The debt transferred with the deed.' Elodie realizes the inheritance was a summons. Emotional beat: grief weaponized.

chapters.title: The Second Chamber
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Deeper in the tunnels, Elodie finds a chamber of preserved belongings — Thomas's watch, her mother's baby shoes, Ruth's long-lost sister's locket. The house keeps what it loves. It loves Elodie already. Emotional beat: the horror of being cherished by something monstrous.

chapters.title: Marion's Confession, Part One
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. A cassette in the study: Marion explains she never wanted the bargain — the house offered, and she said yes because her daughter was dying. She spent fifty years paying interest. Emotional beat: a mother's guilt across the grave.

chapters.title: Wren Asks a Favor
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren asks Elodie to document it — to photograph it, record its voice, write its real name — because being witnessed is the only thing that makes Wren feel real. Elodie agrees. Emotional beat: tenderness as a trap for both of them.

chapters.title: The House Learns Her Routine
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The house begins anticipating her: meals appear, her bed is turned down, her boots are cleaned. Comfort offered by a predator. Ruth stops answering her calls. Emotional beat: domesticity as suffocation.

chapters.title: Tunnel Three: The Throat
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie maps the central shaft — the 'throat' — and hears, far below, voices of everyone the house took, including her grandfather, still speaking, still pleading. She records it. The recording plays back only her own voice. Emotional beat: the futility of evidence against the uncanny.

chapters.title: Marion's Confession, Part Two
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The second cassette reveals the escape clause Marion found but never used: the bargain can be unmade at the hearth, but the one who speaks the reversal must give the house something it values more than the debt. Emotional beat: hope with a hidden invoice.

chapters.title: Ruth Pell, 1968
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, flashback. Ruth remembers the house before it was hungry — a warm, generous place — and the summer it changed, when something was buried beneath the hearth by the original owners. Emotional beat: nostalgia for a house that was once a home.

chapters.title: What's Buried Under the Hearth
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie pries up the hearthstones and finds a child's skeleton, small hands folded around a deed — the original owners' daughter, the house's first taking, the seed of its hunger. Emotional beat: the origin of appetite.

chapters.title: Wren Lies
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren, terrified of being unmade if the bargain reverses, lies to Elodie: it tells her the reversal requires a living body in the throat. Elodie, exhausted, almost believes it. Emotional beat: love curdling into self-preservation.

chapters.title: The House Makes Its Offer
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The house speaks through every surface at once, offering Elodie the same deal Marion got: safety, permanence, the house's devotion — in exchange for becoming its new voice, as Wren is its mouth. Emotional beat: temptation framed as belonging.

chapters.title: Elodie Runs
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie flees to town with her archives. In a motel, she reviews her recordings and finds the house's voice embedded in them, growing clearer each night. It follows the documentation. Emotional beat: the realization that her evidence is a leash.

chapters.title: Ruth's Last Warning
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth finds Elodie and gives her Marion's final letter, never mailed: 'It keeps what is witnessed. Starve it of witness. But no one who does will be remembered, and that is its last cruelty.' Emotional beat: the true price named aloud.

chapters.title: The Archive Burns
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The house, via Wren, destroys Elodie's Detroit storage unit — twenty years of documentation, gone. The message is clear: it will not be starved; it will be fed. Elodie breaks. Emotional beat: despair at the erasure of a life's work.

chapters.title: Wren's True Name
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confesses its real name — Samuel Pell, Ruth's sister's son — and begs Elodie to write it down before the house takes her, so that someone, somewhere, will know he existed. Emotional beat: the hunger for remembrance as the story's beating heart.

chapters.title: A Plan Written in Pencil
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie devises the reversal: speak the original bargain backwards at the hearth, then give the house the only thing it values more than the debt — its own documented history — and burn it, un-witnessing the house into forgetting. Emotional beat: resolve assembled from grief.

chapters.title: The House Fights Back
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Returning, Elodie faces a house that rearranges itself: doors to nowhere, hallways that loop, her childhood bedroom rebuilt around her. She navigates by her old field maps, the one archive the house can't destroy because it lives in her memory. Emotional beat: memory as the last territory.

chapters.title: The Voices Below
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In the throat chamber, the taken speak to her — Thomas asks about Marion, Samuel's voice and Wren's overlap. Elodie promises them remembrance, not rescue, and they go quiet, letting her pass. Emotional beat: compassion as courage.

chapters.title: Wren Chooses
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren intercepts Elodie at the hearth and, instead of stopping her, holds the hearthstones open. If the bargain reverses, Wren ends too — and Wren chooses an ending over an eternity of appetite. Emotional beat: sacrifice as the final act of friendship.

chapters.title: The Reversal
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. At the hearth, Elodie speaks the bargain backwards, word by word, while the house convulses around her. The skeleton beneath the stones is released; the debt is named, refused, and returned. Emotional beat: the climax — a prayer performed as demolition.

chapters.title: What the House Values Most
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. The house demands its price: something it loves. Elodie gives it her complete documentation — every map, tape, and photograph of Hollow Creek — and sets it alight on the hearth. The house, witnessed one last time, is then forgotten. Emotional beat: burning the self to starve the monster.

chapters.title: The House Forgets Itself
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. As the house unravels, Wren feels its hunger dissolve into something like sleep. The walls exhale. Wren, becoming Samuel again for one moment, thanks Elodie before the name dissolves. Emotional beat: peace at the point of annihilation.

chapters.title: Morning Without Hollow Creek
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie wakes on the porch of an ordinary, empty house. The tunnels are gone — solid earth. Her notebooks are blank where Hollow Creek was written. Ruth Pell doesn't know her. Emotional beat: the desolation of a victory no one can share.

chapters.title: The One Page That Survived
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. In her coat pocket, Elodie finds a single page the fire missed: a child's drawing of a girl and a yellow-raincoated friend, signed 'Elodie & Wren, 1994.' The only witness left. Emotional beat: grief and proof held in one hand.

chapters.title: Samuel Pell, In Memoriam
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Elodie tracks down the Pell family history and quietly funds a headstone for Samuel Pell, 'lost 1974,' in the Hollow Creek cemetery. Ruth attends without knowing why she's weeping. Emotional beat: restitution performed in secret.

chapters.title: The Surveyor's New Rule
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. Months later in Detroit, Elodie maps again but keeps no archives — she surveys, memorizes, and lets go. A colleague asks why she never documents anymore. 'Some things stay found if you stop looking at them,' she says. Emotional beat: a changed relationship with witness.

chapters.title: The Porch Light
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV. On the anniversary, Elodie returns to the Hollow Creek property, now sold and renovated. The new owners mention the porch light turns itself on each night at dusk, and they've stopped trying to fix it. Elodie smiles and doesn't explain. Emotional beat: the haunting reduced to a kindness.

chapters.title: What Was Taken, What Was Given
chapters.summary: Elodie's POV, closing. Elodie writes the final entry in a new notebook — not a map, but a letter to Wren, describing the person she became because of what they survived together. She burns it, un-witnessed, and the smoke rises straight up in still air. Emotional beat: love against duty, resolved as release.
